slides.title: Project Overview
slides.blurb: A role-based academic management information system, extended with computer vision and a research-grade neural experiment.

slides.title: What USAMIS Does
slides.sub: One Flask application serving five academic roles
items: Enrolment, academic history, attendance, fees and results in one place
Departments, programmes, courses, semesters and course offerings
Deterministic eligibility rules, credit-weighted GPA, published results
QR session links plus photographed-code decoding with OpenCV
Decimal-safe assessment, payment records and outstanding balances
Generated reports, exports and an immutable audit log

slides.title: The System at a Glance
slides.sub: Measured on the completed demonstration build
slides.note: Roles: Administrator, Registrar, Teacher, Finance Officer, Student and Parent. The parent portal reads a linked student's record and never writes academic data.

slides.title: Scope Discipline
slides.sub: What was added and what was deliberately not
items: OpenCV image scanning, QR POST confirmation, independent neural experiment, logistic comparison, artefact persistence
Deterministic enrolment, grade/GPA and fee algorithms — official records must follow institutional rules
LSTM until genuine weekly sequences exist; face recognition without a validated requirement
Transformers until data scale justifies the complexity
Consented historical snapshots, later-cohort evaluation, calibration checks, human review of alerts

slides.title: The Four Layers
slides.blurb: Logical responsibilities inside a single Flask process — not four separately deployed servers.

slides.title: Layer Responsibilities
slides.sub: Each layer carries independent evidence
rows: Render pages, collect input, display results
Route requests, authenticate, authorise, adapt forms
Apply policy, orchestrate, decode QR, train and infer
Pure algorithm tests; real QR pixels
Store and retrieve records and artefacts

slides.title: Why Four Layers Matters
slides.sub: Separation that is checkable, not just claimed
cards: No framework leakage
Layer 3 algorithms contain no Flask, SQLAlchemy or PostgreSQL imports. They are testable as pure functions.
Repositories, not queries
New code reaches the database through repositories. The neural route calls a service, which calls its repository.
Honest boundaries
Some legacy Flask routes still query the ORM directly. The architecture is a practical separation, not a purity claim.
Independent evidence
Each layer has its own verification scope in verify_layers.ps1, plus integrated request tests on top.
Compile without a server
All Jinja templates compile standalone, proving Layer 1 is not entangled with a running application.
Audit by construction
Every sensitive operation writes an audit row in Layer 4 as part of the same transaction.

slides.title: Layer 3 — Algorithms
slides.blurb: Deterministic policy for official records. Statistical models only for research and support.

slides.title: Deterministic Algorithms
slides.sub: Explainable, reproducible, and auditable by an examiner
items: Checks status, duplicates, prerequisites and capacity. No score, no probability — a rule outcome.
Credit-weighted average of published grades, expressed on the institutional scale.
Decimal-safe arithmetic with explicit status rules, avoiding floating-point drift.
A student's official standing must be defensible to an appeal. Rules can be read, cited and corrected.

slides.title: Probabilistic Components
slides.sub: Where statistical learning is appropriate — and where it is not
items: Computer vision, emphatically not deep learning. A classical detector reads pixels from a photographed code.
A trainable 4–32–16–1 network — this is the deep-learning component of the demonstration.
The same implementation with no hidden layer. A fair, like-for-like baseline.
No model changes a student's grades, enrolment or official academic standing. Ever.

slides.title: QR Attendance
slides.blurb: Acquire attendance reliably, from an image, with signature and replay protection.

slides.title: Request Trace — OpenCV Attendance
slides.sub: One scan, four layers, six steps
items: A signed-in student photographs or uploads the displayed QR image.
The route checks login, the attendance permission and CSRF protection.
OpenCV decodes the image; attendance logic verifies the HMAC signature, expiry, open session and enrolment.
PostgreSQL stores the attendance row and an audit entry in one transaction.
An existing daily record is updated, never duplicated — the operation is idempotent.
The student sees confirmation and their attendance history.

slides.title: Security Properties of Scanning
slides.sub: Deliberate constraints, stated plainly
cards: Processed in memory
The uploaded image is never persisted to disk. Decoding happens entirely in memory.
No URL following
The decoder never follows a URL embedded in an uploaded QR code. Tampered codes are rejected.
POST confirms
An ordinary phone-camera QR link first shows a confirmation page. Only the POST writes attendance.
HMAC signed
Session tokens are signed and time-limited, so a captured token cannot be replayed later.
Idempotent writes
A repeat scan updates the day's record rather than creating a second one.
Honest limitation
Scanning does not prove physical presence, and cannot stop a student sharing an active code.

slides.title: Neural Risk Experiment
slides.blurb: Can earlier academic signals identify students who need support? A measured, honest investigation.

slides.title: The Research Question, Framed Carefully
slides.sub: What this experiment does and does not claim
items: Previous average (0–100), attendance proportion (0–1), early assessment average (0–100), credit load (1–40).
failed_later — an outcome observed strictly after the snapshot date.
Today's cumulative database records are never converted into historical training examples.
The bundled generator creates labelled synthetic examples for teaching only.
60 rows and 15 per class are software minimums, not proof of statistical adequacy.
A reproducible classroom demonstration — not a validated institutional predictor.

slides.title: Model Architecture
slides.sub: A small network, chosen for explainability over complexity
rows: Only signals available at the snapshot date
Sufficient capacity for a small tabular problem
Identical implementation — this is logistic regression

slides.title: Training Configuration
slides.sub: Fixed for reproducibility
slides.note: Loss: binary cross-entropy with L2 regularisation. Best validation-loss weights are restored. Normalisation is fitted on training data only — never on validation or test.

slides.title: Evaluation Protocol
slides.sub: Designed so the test set cannot influence model choice
items: Stratified approximately 60/20/20 across distinct students.
Prevents the same student's examples appearing in both training and test groups.
The comparator is chosen on validation only.
The test group is reported afterwards and does not select the model.
Precision, recall, F1, accuracy, confusion matrix and Brier score.
Scores are not established as calibrated real-world probabilities.

slides.title: Request Trace — Neural Inference
slides.sub: Layer 2 validates, Layer 3 computes, Layer 4 loads
cards: Layer 1
Displays a research form and the held-out results table for comparison.
Layer 2
Permits users holding manage_students, validates the request and handles errors gracefully.
Layer 3
Validates four numerical inputs and performs forward inference.
Layer 4
Loads a versioned JSON artefact, with a PostgreSQL fallback if the file is absent.
Offline training
Reads CSV snapshots and atomically saves the artefact — no partial writes.
Persistence
risk_snapshots and risk_experiments store the dataset and trained bundle in SQL.

slides.title: Verification
slides.blurb: Claims backed by executed checks, not estimates.

slides.title: Evidence
slides.sub: Recorded 30 October 2026 against the live build
slides.note: Full PostgreSQL-backed suite ran in 68.01 seconds. Evidence file: instance/verification.xml. 24 pages plus one neural form submission verified across administrator, teacher, student and parent accounts.

slides.title: What Was Actually Checked
slides.sub: Each item was executed, not assumed
items: All four scopes in scripts/verify_layers.ps1 passed independently.
Tests decode actual QR pixels, persist attendance, reject tampered codes, and confirm repeat scans are idempotent.
Final migration metadata comparison returned an empty diff.
The complete dump restored into a separate empty database; every table count matched.
Eight student and two teacher profiles carry local fictional portraits — display assets, not training data.
A physical-phone classroom trial remains outstanding.

slides.title: Demonstration Database
slides.sub: Restored and row-counted

slides.title: Limitations and Next Steps
slides.blurb: Stated plainly, because a demonstration earns trust by naming its edges.

slides.title: Honest Limitations
slides.sub: What this build does not establish
cards: Synthetic metrics
Model scores come from generated data. They demonstrate method, not institutional truth.
No historical cohort
Real prediction requires consented dated snapshots and later observed outcomes.
Not calibrated
Brier score is reported, but scores are not validated probabilities.
Threshold unset
Choosing an operating threshold depends on advisor capacity — an institutional decision.
External providers
SMS and payment adapters exist; live services were not exercised. Demo records are labelled stub.
Physical trial pending
OpenCV decoding is tested on images, not yet in a live classroom.

slides.title: Recommended Next Steps
slides.sub: In priority order
items: Consented, dated, governance-approved data with later observed outcomes.
Temporal validation is the only meaningful test of a predictor.
Tune the decision boundary to the number of students advisors can actually support.
A DAG with topological sorting can detect cycles and show a valid course order — high value, little data required.
Consider richer sequence models once genuine weekly sequences exist.

slides.heading: Questions
lines: USAMIS runs locally at http://127.0.0.1:5055 — a classroom demonstration with fictional people and synthetic training data.
Four layers, one process. Deterministic rules for official records. Statistical models for support, never authority.
194 tests passed. Four layer scopes verified. Every claim in this deck is reproducible from the repository.
